title: An extraordinarily slender galaxy
caption: The edge-on galaxy NGC 4452, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A bright nucleus sits at the centre of a disc so thin it looks like a straight line in this Hubble image of NGC 4452. A hazy halo of stars around the galaxy makes it seem to glow. We see it almost exactly edge-on from Earth, an unusual angle on its billions of stars.
William Herschel first spotted NGC 4452 in 1784, using his 47 cm telescope in England, describing it as a bright nebula, small and very elongated. Hubble shows just how elongated it really is.

NGC 4452 belongs to the Virgo Cluster, an enormous grouping of around 2000 galaxies approximately 60 million light-years away. Our own Local Group is thought to lie on the cluster's fringes, and far in the future it may be pulled slowly into Virgo by gravity. Many faint galaxies much farther away appear in the background.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. A blue filter is coloured blue and a near-infrared filter is coloured red.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's long exposures reveal faint background galaxies no eye could see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Edwin Hubble, for whom the telescope is named, was the first to prove that other galaxies exist beyond our own, by measuring their distances in the 1920s. The image's field of view spans 2.6 arcminutes.
alt: An extremely thin, edge-on galaxy that looks like a straight line of light with a bright centre and hazy halo, with faint galaxies in the background.
